```json
{
  "winner": "A",
  "reasons": [
    "Price per customer favors A. Its self-serve anchors run $19-199/mo, with Agentshield at $49/mo. B's anchors run $4.99-7/mo. Landing one paying customer in 90 days is more valuable and more plausible where the buyer is a team with a budget, not a financially stressed individual.",
    "A's demand evidence includes a documented public incident: PocketOS, where an agent deleted a production database and its backups in nine seconds. It also has two independent developer quotes about the pain. B's demand quotes are weaker. One comes from a person who built a competing app, and another says the app would be useful only 'as long as it's free'.",
    "A has a cheap channel that matches the buyer. A Show HN or open-source launch reaches engineers directly, and self-serve tiers let them buy without procurement. B's cheap organic channel, Reddit caregiver communities, is shown to already favor an incumbent (three unsolicited Caring Village recommendations). Its paid channel is backed only by a generic 2017 Facebook CPC benchmark.",
    "B carries structural headwinds the brief documents itself. Multi-sibling activation friction, short customer lifetimes that end when the parent's care situation ends, and users who explicitly want it free all slow the path to a first payment.",
    "A's biggest risks are the same kind as B's crowding risk. A faces 9+ competitors, free OSS alternatives, and SOC 2/trust barriers. The SOC 2 barrier mainly blocks enterprise deals, though, and does not clearly block a $19-49/mo self-serve sale to a small team."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "Idea B's lead demand quote ('Google Calendar and group threads weren't really built for caregiving. That's why I built [an app]...') comes from a builder promoting their own app, not a buyer stating unmet need. It is evidence of supply, not demand. It is paired with a second quote that conditions interest on the app being free, which argues against willingness to pay.",
  "confidence_note": "Moderate-to-low confidence. Both briefs describe crowded fields, and neither shows direct evidence that a new entrant converted a first paying customer. A's demand quotes express fear and preference, not willingness to pay. A's trust/SOC 2 barrier and free OSS competition could block even self-serve sales. The pick rests mainly on A's higher per-customer price and B's weaker demand quotes, not on strong positive evidence for A."
}
```
